name: Tulsi
shortDescription: Aromatic herb with major cultural and traditional importance in Ayurveda.
description: Tulsi is a much-branched, strongly aromatic herb or small shrub found across India and grown in most Kerala households, often in a dedicated courtyard planter. It holds deep religious and cultural significance in Hindu tradition and is one of the most widely referenced plants in Ayurvedic literature.

identification.leaves: Simple, ovate leaves with a toothed margin, arranged oppositely; strongly aromatic when crushed.
identification.flowers: Small purplish or white flowers borne on elongated terminal spikes.
identification.fruit: Tiny nutlets that form after flowering, not commonly used.
identification.stem: Erect, branching, slightly woody at the base, green to purplish in colour.

traditionalKnowledge: In traditional and Ayurvedic practice, Tulsi leaves are used in herbal teas and are considered sacred, associated with purification and everyday household rituals.
habitat: Grows well in warm, tropical climates with moderate rainfall and good sunlight.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Indian subcontinent; widely cultivated throughout India, including Kerala.
cultivation: Easily grown from seed or cuttings in pots or garden beds; prefers well-drained soil and regular watering.
safety: Generally regarded as safe for culinary and ceremonial use in small amounts; those on medication should consult a healthcare provider before regular herbal use.

name: Neem
shortDescription: Evergreen tree widely known for its traditional uses and cultural significance.
description: Neem is a fast-growing evergreen tree common across the Indian plains and cultivated in South India for shade and its traditionally valued leaves, bark and seeds. It is a familiar sight in villages and temple grounds and has long been associated with traditional hygiene practices.

identification.leaves: Pinnately compound leaves with serrated, pointed leaflets.
identification.flowers: Small, fragrant white flowers arranged in clusters.
identification.fruit: Smooth, olive-like drupe that ripens from green to yellow.
identification.stem: Straight trunk with rough, fissured, greyish-brown bark.

traditionalKnowledge: Various parts of the neem tree have a long history of use in traditional Indian practices, particularly related to skin and household applications; neem twigs have traditionally been used for oral hygiene.
habitat: Thrives in tropical and subtropical climates, tolerant of dry and poor soils.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Indian subcontinent; common throughout India.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; drought-tolerant once established and requires minimal maintenance.
safety: Neem oil and seed extracts are potent and are not intended for internal use without professional guidance; keep away from young children.

name: Aloe Vera
shortDescription: Succulent plant recognized for its gel and long history in traditional practices.
description: Aloe vera is a stemless or short-stemmed succulent with thick, fleshy leaves that store a clear gel. It is grown widely in home gardens across Kerala and South India and is a familiar plant in both traditional herbal practice and modern personal care products.

identification.leaves: Thick, fleshy, lance-shaped leaves with serrated edges, arranged in a rosette.
identification.flowers: Tubular yellow flowers borne on a tall spike, though flowering is infrequent in cultivation.
identification.fruit: Not typically grown for fruit; occasional small capsule fruit after flowering.
identification.stem: Very short or absent, with leaves emerging directly near ground level.

traditionalKnowledge: The clear inner gel has a long history of topical traditional use for skin care, and the plant is a staple of home herbal gardens across South Asia.
habitat: Prefers warm, dry conditions with well-drained soil; tolerates drought well.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Believed to originate from the Arabian Peninsula; naturalised and widely cultivated across India.
cultivation: Easily propagated from offsets; needs minimal watering and full to partial sun.
safety: Topical use of the gel is generally well tolerated; the yellow latex near the leaf skin can be irritating and is usually removed before use. Consult a professional before internal use.

name: Turmeric
shortDescription: Rhizomatous plant valued as a spice and for its traditional Ayurvedic importance.
description: Turmeric is a rhizomatous perennial herb cultivated throughout India for its bright yellow-orange underground rhizome, a defining ingredient of South Indian cuisine and a plant with deep cultural and Ayurvedic significance in Kerala.

identification.leaves: Large, broad, lance-shaped leaves arising directly from the rhizome.
identification.flowers: Pale yellow flowers enclosed within pink or green bracts, borne on a central spike.
identification.fruit: Rarely produces viable fruit in cultivation; propagated vegetatively.
identification.stem: Underground, forming a branched, aromatic rhizome; the visible 'stem' is a leaf sheath.

traditionalKnowledge: The rhizome has a long history of culinary and traditional Ayurvedic use in India, including in ceremonial and household contexts.
habitat: Requires warm, humid climates with well-drained, fertile soil.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to South Asia; extensively cultivated across India, including Kerala.
cultivation: Propagated from rhizome pieces; harvested after the leaves die back, typically 8–10 months after planting.
safety: Widely used as a food spice and generally considered safe in culinary amounts; concentrated extracts should be used only under professional guidance.

name: Ginger
shortDescription: Aromatic rhizome commonly used as a spice and in traditional herbal preparations.
description: Ginger is a perennial herb grown for its pungent, aromatic rhizome, a key ingredient in South Indian cooking and traditional preparations. It is widely cultivated in Kerala's hill regions.

identification.leaves: Long, narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately along the stem.
identification.flowers: Yellow-green flowers with purple markings, borne on a separate short spike; flowering is uncommon in cultivation.
identification.fruit: Rarely fruits in cultivation; grown for its rhizome.
identification.stem: Slender, reed-like pseudostem formed by overlapping leaf sheaths.

traditionalKnowledge: The rhizome is a staple culinary spice with a long history of traditional use in warming preparations and herbal drinks across India.
habitat: Grows best in warm, humid climates with rich, well-drained soil and partial shade.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to Southeast Asia; extensively cultivated across India, including Kerala and the Western Ghats.
cultivation: Propagated from rhizome pieces; harvested roughly 8–10 months after planting.
safety: Commonly consumed as a food spice; concentrated forms may interact with certain medications, so professional advice is recommended for medicinal use.

name: Ashwagandha
shortDescription: Traditional Ayurvedic herb known for its long history in Indian herbal practices.
description: Ashwagandha is a small, woody shrub whose roots are among the most referenced botanicals in classical Ayurvedic literature. It is cultivated in parts of India for traditional herbal use.

identification.leaves: Simple, ovate, slightly hairy leaves arranged alternately.
identification.flowers: Small, greenish-yellow, bell-shaped flowers.
identification.fruit: Small orange-red berries enclosed in a papery calyx.
identification.stem: Erect, branching, covered in fine hairs.

traditionalKnowledge: The root is a central herb in classical Ayurvedic texts, traditionally described within the category of rejuvenating tonics.
habitat: Grows in dry, subtropical regions with well-drained soil.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to India, the Middle East and parts of Africa; cultivated across several Indian states.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; prefers a dry climate and sandy loam soil.
safety: Should be used only under professional guidance, particularly during pregnancy or alongside other medications, as it is a potent traditional root.

name: Amla
shortDescription: Fruit-bearing tree traditionally valued for its nutritional and Ayurvedic importance.
description: Amla, also called Indian Gooseberry, is a deciduous tree bearing small, translucent green fruits that are a well-known feature of Ayurvedic tradition and South Indian cuisine. It is commonly grown in home gardens across Kerala.

identification.leaves: Small, feathery, closely spaced leaflets giving a fern-like appearance.
identification.flowers: Small, greenish-yellow flowers clustered along the branchlets.
identification.fruit: Round, pale green, translucent fruit with a sharp, sour taste.
identification.stem: Greyish bark that peels in thin flakes; slender branches.

traditionalKnowledge: The fruit has a long history of use in Ayurvedic preparations and in traditional pickles and preserves across India.
habitat: Grows in a range of soils from dry to moist, tolerating both drought and mild waterlogging.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Indian subcontinent; widely grown throughout India, including Kerala.
cultivation: Propagated by grafting or seed; fruits are harvested in the cooler months.
safety: The fresh fruit is commonly eaten as food; concentrated extracts should be used with professional guidance.

name: Brahmi
shortDescription: Small creeping herb traditionally associated with learning and cognitive wellness.
description: Brahmi is a small, succulent, creeping herb that grows in wet or marshy ground and is one of the most referenced herbs in Ayurvedic tradition, particularly in the context of study and memory.

identification.leaves: Small, fleshy, oblong leaves arranged oppositely along creeping stems.
identification.flowers: Small, pale purple to white flowers with four to five petals.
identification.fruit: Small oval capsule containing tiny seeds.
identification.stem: Soft, succulent, creeping and rooting at the nodes.

traditionalKnowledge: Classical Ayurvedic tradition describes Brahmi as a herb associated with mental clarity and learning; it remains a subject of ongoing scientific research.
habitat: Grows in wet, marshy soils, riverbanks and shallow water.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to South Asia and other wetland regions; found across India, including Kerala's waterlogged areas.
cultivation: Propagated from stem cuttings; requires consistently moist soil or shallow water.
safety: Generally used in traditional low-dose preparations; professional guidance is recommended, especially for children and pregnant women.

name: Moringa
shortDescription: Nutrient-rich tree whose leaves, pods and other parts have many traditional uses.
description: Moringa, known locally as the drumstick tree, is a fast-growing tree cultivated throughout Kerala for its nutrient-dense leaves and long, ridged seed pods, both staples of South Indian cooking.

identification.leaves: Compound, feathery leaves divided into small oval leaflets.
identification.flowers: Small, fragrant, cream-white flowers borne in loose clusters.
identification.fruit: Long, slender, ridged pods known as 'drumsticks', containing round seeds.
identification.stem: Soft, pale, corky bark; brittle branches.

traditionalKnowledge: Various parts of the moringa tree have a long history of traditional and culinary use across South Asia and Africa.
habitat: Grows in a wide range of tropical and subtropical soils; tolerant of drought.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the sub-Himalayan regions of India; widely cultivated across Kerala and South India.
cultivation: Easily grown from seed or stem cuttings; fast-growing and low maintenance.
safety: Leaves and pods are widely eaten as food; the root and root bark are traditionally used with caution and are not recommended without professional guidance.

name: Curry Leaf
shortDescription: Aromatic tree whose leaves are widely used in Indian cooking and traditional practices.
description: The curry leaf tree is a small aromatic tree grown in nearly every South Indian kitchen garden. Its fragrant leaves are a defining ingredient of Kerala and South Indian cuisine.

identification.leaves: Pinnately compound leaves with small, glossy, aromatic leaflets.
identification.flowers: Small, white, fragrant flowers borne in clusters.
identification.fruit: Small, shiny black berries when ripe, not typically eaten.
identification.stem: Slender, greyish-brown, branching stem.

traditionalKnowledge: The aromatic leaves are used fresh in daily cooking across South India and have a place in traditional household herbal knowledge.
habitat: Grows well in tropical and subtropical climates with moderate rainfall.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to India and Sri Lanka; a common kitchen-garden plant throughout South India.
cultivation: Propagated from seed or root suckers; prefers well-drained, fertile soil and partial sun.
safety: Leaves are widely consumed as a culinary herb and are generally considered safe in normal food quantities.

name: Lemongrass
shortDescription: Fragrant grass commonly used in food, beverages and traditional herbal practices.
description: Lemongrass is a tall, tufted aromatic grass with a distinct citrus fragrance, widely grown in Kerala home gardens and used in teas, cooking and traditional preparations.

identification.leaves: Long, narrow, blade-like leaves with a sharp edge and strong lemon scent when crushed.
identification.flowers: Rarely flowers in cultivation; when present, forms tall, loose flower spikes.
identification.fruit: Not grown for fruit.
identification.stem: Fibrous, clustered stem base forming dense tufts.

traditionalKnowledge: Traditionally brewed as a fragrant herbal tea and used in South and Southeast Asian cooking for its citrus aroma.
habitat: Grows well in warm, tropical climates with moderate to high rainfall.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to South and Southeast Asia; widely cultivated across Kerala.
cultivation: Propagated by dividing established clumps; low maintenance and drought-tolerant once established.
safety: Commonly consumed as a herbal tea in moderate amounts; the essential oil is concentrated and not intended for direct internal use.

name: Mint
shortDescription: Aromatic herb widely used in food and traditional preparations.
description: Mint is a fast-spreading, fragrant herb grown widely across India for culinary use, from chutneys to beverages, and is a familiar plant in Kerala home gardens.

identification.leaves: Simple, opposite, toothed leaves with a strong, refreshing aroma.
identification.flowers: Small, pale purple or white flowers borne in whorled clusters.
identification.fruit: Tiny nutlets, not commonly used.
identification.stem: Square, spreading, often rooting at the nodes.

traditionalKnowledge: Widely used fresh in South Asian cooking and traditional herbal drinks for its cooling, refreshing character.
habitat: Prefers moist, well-drained soil and partial shade to full sun.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Various Mentha species are native to Europe, Asia and Africa; widely cultivated across India.
cultivation: Propagated easily from cuttings or runners; spreads readily and needs regular watering.
safety: Widely consumed as a culinary herb; generally well tolerated in normal food amounts.

name: Hibiscus
shortDescription: Flowering plant valued ornamentally and in several traditional preparations.
description: Hibiscus is a popular flowering shrub grown throughout Kerala for its large, showy blooms, seen in gardens, temple offerings and traditional hair-care preparations.

identification.leaves: Glossy, dark green, toothed, ovate leaves.
identification.flowers: Large, funnel-shaped flowers, most commonly red, with a prominent central staminal column.
identification.fruit: Small dry capsule, rarely of interest.
identification.stem: Woody, branching shrub stem.

traditionalKnowledge: Flowers and leaves have a long-standing place in traditional South Indian hair-care and are commonly offered in temple rituals.
habitat: Grows well in warm, humid, tropical conditions with regular watering.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to East Asia; naturalised and extremely common throughout India, including Kerala.
cultivation: Propagated from stem cuttings; needs full sun and regular watering for best flowering.
safety: Generally regarded as safe for topical and traditional external use; not intended for internal medicinal use without guidance.

name: Ashoka
shortDescription: Sacred Indian tree with a long history in Ayurvedic and cultural traditions.
description: Ashoka is a small to medium evergreen tree revered in Indian tradition and mentioned frequently in classical literature and Ayurvedic texts, often planted near temples.

identification.leaves: Long, pinnately compound leaves with lance-shaped leaflets that droop when young.
identification.flowers: Bright orange-yellow to red, fragrant flowers borne in dense clusters.
identification.fruit: Flat, woody seed pod.
identification.stem: Smooth, dark grey-brown bark.

traditionalKnowledge: The bark holds a prominent place in classical Ayurvedic tradition and the tree itself carries deep cultural and religious symbolism.
habitat: Grows in moist, shaded conditions, often near riverbanks.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Indian subcontinent; found in Kerala's forests and temple gardens.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; prefers partial shade and consistently moist soil when young.
safety: Bark preparations are traditionally used under professional guidance; the tree is also of conservation concern in parts of its range.

name: Arjuna
shortDescription: Large tree traditionally important in Ayurveda, particularly its bark.
description: Arjuna is a large, buttressed deciduous tree commonly found along riverbanks, its smooth, pale bark holding a prominent place in classical Ayurvedic tradition.

identification.leaves: Oblong leaves, dark green above and pale beneath, arranged sub-oppositely.
identification.flowers: Small, pale yellow flowers borne in short spikes.
identification.fruit: Woody, five-winged fruit.
identification.stem: Smooth, pale grey to pinkish bark that flakes in patches; often buttressed at the base.

traditionalKnowledge: The bark is one of the most referenced botanicals in classical Ayurvedic cardiovascular tradition, distinct from established modern medical treatment.
habitat: Grows well along riverbanks and in moist deciduous forests.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Indian subcontinent; found across peninsular India, including Kerala.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; prefers moist soil and does well near water bodies.
safety: Bark preparations should only be used under qualified professional guidance.

name: Licorice
shortDescription: Root-bearing herb traditionally used in various herbal preparations.
description: Licorice is a perennial herb valued for its sweet-tasting roots, traditionally used across Indian herbal systems and often included in throat-soothing preparations.

identification.leaves: Pinnately compound leaves with several pairs of small leaflets.
identification.flowers: Small, pale purple to whitish pea-like flowers in spikes.
identification.fruit: Small, flattened, oblong pod.
identification.stem: Erect, herbaceous to slightly woody stem.

traditionalKnowledge: The root has a long tradition of use in soothing herbal preparations across South Asian and Middle Eastern herbal systems.
habitat: Prefers deep, well-drained soils in sunny, temperate to subtropical locations.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Mediterranean and parts of Asia; cultivated in parts of India for traditional use.
cultivation: Propagated from root divisions or seed; requires deep soil for good root development.
safety: Excessive or prolonged use is not advised, particularly for those with high blood pressure; professional guidance is recommended.

name: Shatavari
shortDescription: Traditional Ayurvedic plant with tuberous roots and cultural importance.
description: Shatavari is a climbing, thorny plant with clusters of tuberous roots, one of the most referenced herbs in classical Ayurvedic tradition relating to women's wellness.

identification.leaves: Fine, needle-like cladodes (modified leaf-like stems) arranged in clusters.
identification.flowers: Small, fragrant white flowers.
identification.fruit: Small, round, red berry.
identification.stem: Wiry, climbing, thorny stem.

traditionalKnowledge: The tuberous root is central to classical Ayurvedic tradition and is described within the category of traditional rejuvenating tonics.
habitat: Grows in scrub forests and rocky, well-drained terrain.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Indian subcontinent; found across India, including Kerala's forest margins.
cultivation: Propagated from root divisions or seed; needs support for its climbing habit.
safety: Should be used under professional guidance, particularly during pregnancy or alongside medication.

name: Guduchi
shortDescription: Climbing plant widely recognized in traditional Indian herbal knowledge.
description: Guduchi is a deciduous climbing shrub with a distinctive heart-shaped leaf, widely recognised across Indian herbal tradition and often referred to by its Sanskrit name meaning 'that which protects the body'.

identification.leaves: Heart-shaped, glossy green leaves.
identification.flowers: Small, greenish-yellow flowers borne in racemes.
identification.fruit: Small, red, pea-sized drupe when ripe.
identification.stem: Succulent, fleshy, twining stem with warty bark.

traditionalKnowledge: The stem holds an important place in classical Ayurvedic tradition and is one of the most widely referenced climbing plants in Indian herbal knowledge.
habitat: Grows in deciduous forests and thrives when climbing on host trees.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Indian subcontinent; found across India, including Kerala.
cultivation: Propagated from stem cuttings; needs a support structure or host tree to climb.
safety: Should be used under professional guidance; not recommended for self-medication.

name: Gotu Kola
shortDescription: Creeping herb traditionally used in South and Southeast Asian herbal practices.
description: Gotu Kola is a small, creeping herb found in moist, shaded areas across Kerala, traditionally valued in South and Southeast Asian herbal systems and sometimes confused with the unrelated herb Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri).

identification.leaves: Small, rounded to kidney-shaped leaves with scalloped edges, borne on long stalks.
identification.flowers: Tiny, pinkish-white flowers borne close to the ground.
identification.fruit: Small, ribbed, oval fruit.
identification.stem: Slender, creeping stem that roots at the nodes.

traditionalKnowledge: Traditionally used across South and Southeast Asian herbal systems and, in some regional traditions, associated with mental clarity in a manner similar to Bacopa monnieri.
habitat: Grows in moist, shaded or marshy ground, often near water.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to wetland regions of Asia; common across Kerala's moist habitats.
cultivation: Propagated from stem cuttings or runners; needs consistent moisture.
safety: Generally used in traditional low-dose preparations; professional guidance is recommended for regular use.

name: Vetiver
shortDescription: Fragrant grass valued for its aromatic roots and traditional applications.
description: Vetiver is a tall, tufted perennial grass with a dense network of aromatic roots, traditionally used in Kerala for cooling mats, screens and fragrant preparations, especially during summer.

identification.leaves: Long, narrow, stiff leaves with a rough texture.
identification.flowers: Loose, purplish-brown flower spikelets, rarely prominent.
identification.fruit: Not grown for fruit.
identification.stem: Dense, fibrous tufted stem base with deep, aromatic roots.

traditionalKnowledge: The aromatic roots have a long tradition of use in Kerala for cooling window screens, mats and fragrant water preparations during the hot season.
habitat: Grows in a wide range of soils, tolerant of both wet and dry conditions.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to India; widely cultivated across South India, including Kerala.
cultivation: Propagated by root or slip division; deep-rooted and useful for soil stabilisation.
safety: Primarily used for its fragrance in traditional applications; not intended for internal medicinal use.

name: Black Pepper
shortDescription: Climbing vine producing a major Indian spice with traditional significance.
description: Black pepper is a woody, climbing vine native to the Western Ghats of Kerala, historically known as the 'King of Spices' and central to the region's spice trade history.

identification.leaves: Broad, glossy, heart-shaped leaves arranged alternately.
identification.flowers: Small, tightly clustered flowers on a hanging spike.
identification.fruit: Small, round drupe that turns from green to red and is dried to produce the familiar peppercorn.
identification.stem: Woody, climbing stem that attaches to support trees or poles via small roots.

traditionalKnowledge: Peppercorns are a defining South Indian spice with an extensive history of culinary and traditional use across Kerala.
habitat: Thrives in humid, tropical climates with well-drained soil and partial shade.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Western Ghats of Kerala; a signature crop of the Kerala spice belt.
cultivation: Propagated from stem cuttings, trained to climb support trees or poles; harvested when berries begin to redden.
safety: Widely used as a food spice; generally safe in normal culinary quantities.

name: Cardamom
shortDescription: Aromatic spice plant native to the Western Ghats and important in Kerala.
description: Cardamom, often called the 'Queen of Spices', is a rhizomatous perennial native to the high-altitude forests of Kerala's Western Ghats, prized for its fragrant seed pods.

identification.leaves: Long, lance-shaped leaves arranged in two rows along leafy shoots.
identification.flowers: Small, whitish flowers with purple-veined lips, borne on separate flowering stalks.
identification.fruit: Small, ridged, oval capsule containing dark aromatic seeds.
identification.stem: Underground rhizome with tall, reed-like leafy shoots.

traditionalKnowledge: The aromatic seed pods are central to South Indian cuisine and traditional preparations, and are a historic export crop of Kerala.
habitat: Requires cool, humid, high-altitude forest conditions with filtered shade.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Western Ghats of Kerala and Karnataka; grown extensively in Kerala's cardamom hills.
cultivation: Propagated from rhizome division or seedlings; grown under forest canopy shade at higher elevations.
safety: Widely used as a food spice; generally safe in normal culinary quantities.

name: Cinnamon
shortDescription: Aromatic tree whose bark is widely used as a spice and in traditional practices.
description: Cinnamon is an evergreen tree cultivated in Kerala for its fragrant inner bark, which is dried and rolled into the familiar cinnamon quills used in cooking and traditional preparations.

identification.leaves: Glossy, leathery, elliptical leaves with three prominent veins.
identification.flowers: Small, pale yellow-green flowers borne in clusters.
identification.fruit: Small, dark purple, single-seeded berry.
identification.stem: Inner bark is aromatic and is harvested and dried to form cinnamon quills.

traditionalKnowledge: The bark has an extensive history as a South Indian spice and in traditional warming preparations.
habitat: Grows in warm, humid, tropical lowland conditions.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to Sri Lanka and South India; cultivated in Kerala's spice-growing regions.
cultivation: Propagated from seed or cuttings; bark is harvested periodically from mature stems.
safety: Widely used as a food spice; generally safe in normal culinary quantities.

name: Clove
shortDescription: Aromatic flower bud used as a spice and in traditional herbal preparations.
description: Clove is an evergreen tree grown in Kerala for its aromatic flower buds, which are hand-picked and dried to produce the familiar dark brown spice used across South Indian cuisine.

identification.leaves: Glossy, elliptical, aromatic leaves arranged oppositely.
identification.flowers: Buds are harvested before opening; if left, they open into small pinkish flowers.
identification.fruit: Not grown for fruit; the unopened flower bud is the harvested part.
identification.stem: Smooth, greyish bark on a moderately tall evergreen tree.

traditionalKnowledge: The dried flower bud has a long tradition of culinary use and is traditionally associated with oral and dental comfort in South Indian households.
habitat: Requires warm, humid, tropical conditions with well-drained soil.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia; cultivated in Kerala's spice belt.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; buds are hand-harvested just before flowering and sun-dried.
safety: Widely used as a food spice in small quantities; concentrated clove oil is potent and not intended for undiluted use.

name: Indian Bay Leaf
shortDescription: Aromatic tree whose leaves are used as a spice in South Asian cuisine.
description: Indian Bay Leaf is an evergreen tree closely related to cinnamon, grown for its aromatic leaves, which are a common flavouring in South Asian rice and curry dishes.

identification.leaves: Glossy, leathery leaves with three prominent longitudinal veins, aromatic when crushed.
identification.flowers: Small, pale yellow-green flowers in clusters.
identification.fruit: Small, dark, single-seeded berry.
identification.stem: Smooth, aromatic bark similar to that of true cinnamon.

traditionalKnowledge: The dried leaves are a common flavouring herb in South Asian cooking, distinct from the Mediterranean bay leaf (Laurus nobilis).
habitat: Grows in warm, humid subtropical to tropical climates.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Himalayan foothills and Northeast India; cultivated in parts of South India.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; leaves are harvested and dried for culinary use.
safety: Widely used as a food spice; generally safe in normal culinary quantities.

name: Fenugreek
shortDescription: Herb whose seeds and leaves are commonly used as food and in traditional practices.
description: Fenugreek is an annual herb grown for its aromatic seeds and edible leaves, both widely used in South Indian cooking and traditional household preparations.

identification.leaves: Trifoliate leaves with small, oval, slightly toothed leaflets.
identification.flowers: Small, pale yellow to white pea-like flowers.
identification.fruit: Long, slender, curved pod containing small, hard, angular seeds.
identification.stem: Erect, slender, herbaceous stem.

traditionalKnowledge: The seeds and leaves have an extensive history of use in South Asian cooking and household herbal traditions.
habitat: Prefers cooler, well-drained conditions, often grown as a cool-season crop.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Mediterranean region and Western Asia; widely cultivated across India.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; grows quickly and is often harvested young for leaves.
safety: Widely used as a food spice and vegetable; generally safe in normal culinary quantities.

name: Coriander
shortDescription: Aromatic herb widely used for its leaves and seeds in cooking and traditional preparations.
description: Coriander is an annual herb grown throughout Kerala for its fragrant leaves and seeds, both essential ingredients in South Indian cooking.

identification.leaves: Feathery, finely divided upper leaves and broader lower leaves.
identification.flowers: Small white to pale pink flowers borne in flat-topped clusters.
identification.fruit: Small, round, ridged seed capsule (used as the spice).
identification.stem: Slender, hollow, branching stem.

traditionalKnowledge: Leaves and seeds have an extensive history of daily culinary use across South Asian households.
habitat: Grows well in cool weather with well-drained, fertile soil.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Mediterranean and Western Asia; widely cultivated across India.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; grows quickly and is harvested young for leaves or left to mature for seed.
safety: Widely used as a food herb and spice; generally safe in normal culinary quantities.

name: Cumin
shortDescription: Aromatic seed-producing plant commonly used as a spice and in traditional food practices.
description: Cumin is a small annual herb cultivated for its aromatic seeds, a staple spice across Indian cooking, including South Indian tempering and traditional preparations.

identification.leaves: Finely divided, thread-like leaves.
identification.flowers: Small white or pink flowers borne in umbels.
identification.fruit: Small, ridged, oblong seed used as the spice.
identification.stem: Slender, branching, herbaceous stem.

traditionalKnowledge: Cumin seeds are a foundational spice across Indian cuisine, with a long history of daily culinary and traditional household use.
habitat: Prefers hot, dry conditions with well-drained soil.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Eastern Mediterranean and South Asia; cultivated across India.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; requires a relatively dry growing season for good seed set.
safety: Widely used as a food spice; generally safe in normal culinary quantities.

name: Bael
shortDescription: Sacred tree whose fruits and leaves have important cultural and traditional uses.
description: Bael is a medium-sized, spiny deciduous tree revered in Indian tradition and commonly planted near temples, valued for its aromatic, hard-shelled fruit and trifoliate leaves used in religious offerings.

identification.leaves: Trifoliate leaves with aromatic, slightly toothed leaflets.
identification.flowers: Small, fragrant, greenish-white flowers.
identification.fruit: Hard-shelled, round fruit with a sweet, aromatic pulp when ripe.
identification.stem: Grey, often spiny bark with a somewhat irregular branching pattern.

traditionalKnowledge: The fruit and leaves have deep religious significance in Indian tradition and a long history of traditional culinary use.
habitat: Tolerant of a wide range of soils and climates, including dry conditions.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the Indian subcontinent; found across India, including Kerala's temple groves.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; hardy and low maintenance once established.
safety: The ripe fruit pulp is commonly consumed as food; unripe fruit is generally avoided as food due to its astringency.

name: Malabar Nut
shortDescription: Shrub traditionally recognized in Ayurveda and known for its distinctive leaves and flowers.
description: Malabar Nut is an evergreen shrub with large, lance-shaped leaves, widely recognised in Ayurvedic tradition and commonly found growing wild along field edges in Kerala.

identification.leaves: Large, lance-shaped, opposite leaves with a slightly rough texture.

name: Indian Long Pepper
shortDescription: Climbing plant producing a traditional spice important in Ayurvedic herbal knowledge.

identification.fruit: Small fruits fused into a compact, cylindrical spike, harvested and dried whole as the spice.

name: Guggul

identification.flowers: Small, reddish flowers, inconspicuous.
identification.fruit: Small, reddish, oval fruit.
identification.stem: Thorny, knotted branches that exude an aromatic gum resin when wounded.

traditionalKnowledge: The gum resin holds a prominent place in classical Ayurvedic tradition and is also traditionally used in incense preparations.
habitat: Adapted to arid and semi-arid conditions with sparse rainfall.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to the dry regions of northwestern India; the resin is traded across India for traditional use.
cultivation: Propagated from cuttings; requires a dry, well-drained environment and minimal watering.
safety: Traditional resin preparations should be used only under professional guidance; the species is also of conservation concern in parts of its native range.

name: Kalmegh
shortDescription: Bitter herb widely known in traditional Indian herbal systems.

identification.stem: Erect, slender, four-angled stem.

habitat: Grows in moist, shaded areas, often as a wild or cultivated herb.
nativeOrCommonRegion: Native to South and Southeast Asia; common in Kerala's moist lowlands.
cultivation: Propagated from seed; grows readily in moist, partially shaded conditions.
safety: Traditional preparations should be used under professional guidance rather than self-administered.

name: Punarnava

identification.stem: Slender, erect, woody stem.

habitat: Grows in moist, shaded forest understories.

name: Sandalwood
